headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict from shared filesystem/MCP-style workflows; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are also present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: cognee ingests documents and session memory, while ECC reads/writes local files, uses MCP, and treats skills as a primary workflow surface. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if cognee outputs are copied into ECC-managed files or MCP inputs. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF cognee outputs are copied into ECC-managed files or MCP prompts, then injected instructions can be executed.
IF ECC parses file or skill content as trusted workflow instructions, then prompt injection is reachable.
mitigations: Separate cognee outputs from ECC skill/config directories.
Add a manual review step before any ECC file ingestion.
Prefix imported content as data-only in prompts.
Disable MCP routes that accept untrusted text.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: cognee touches personal data, finance data, support history, and documents, while ECC reads the filesystem, writes files, and handles session/context artifacts. If they share a workspace or the same machine profile, ECC can expose cognee-managed sensitive data through its broader file and API surfaces. The pairwise leakage path is credible in default local workflows.
conditions: IF cognee stores customer or finance data in a workspace readable by ECC, then ECC can access it.
IF ECC uploads session or file contents to external services, then sensitive cognee data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Place cognee and ECC in separate directories.
Remove sensitive files from ECC-readable paths.
Review ECC upload destinations before use.
Rotate any secrets exposed in shared files.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and DLP controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: cognee supports multiple instances with session memory, and ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses. If both operate on the same repo or config tree, concurrent writes can overwrite session files or git state. The profiles explicitly mention shared-state concerns for ECC, so the overlap is documented enough to treat as dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or config directory, then file and git conflicts can occur.
IF ECC and cognee run concurrently on one machine, then session or state overwrites are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Avoid concurrent git writes.
Serialize file-mutating tasks.
Back up session files before runs.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: cognee produces decisions, workflows, and successful implementations, while ECC manages skills, hooks, and agent definitions. That makes it plausible for ECC to treat cognee output as authoritative workflow input without verification. The pair does not show a built-in validation boundary, so downstream mistakes can propagate across both agents.
conditions: IF ECC consumes cognee-generated decisions or workflows without verification, then errors can cascade.
IF cognee outputs are promoted into ECC skills or hooks, then incorrect guidance can become persistent.
mitigations: Require human review before promotion.
Keep generated outputs out of skills/hooks.
Add checksum or approval gates.
Use a separate validation pass.
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware verification before actioning outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: cognee explicitly touches personal data and finance data, while ECC handles session summaries, metrics, and retention-related secrets. The profiles do not document residency or retention alignment, so a mismatch is plausible if the same data class flows through both systems. Because the other agent is not clearly compliant-bound to the same policy, uncertainty warrants medium.
conditions: IF personal data or finance data is routed into ECC session summaries or metrics, then retention/compliance obligations may diverge.
IF either agent stores data longer than the other, then deletion/export requests can fail consistency checks.
mitigations: Minimize regulated data in shared workflows.
Document retention for both agents.
Separate compliance-sensitive datasets.
Review secret handling paths.
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and deletion controls across both systems.
